analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate drug prices directly and lets Americans import cheaper prescriptions from Canada.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2004 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill was a Democratic rewrite of the Medicare drug benefit that Congress passed in 2003. It would have let the Secretary of Health and Human Services negotiate drug prices directly with manufacturers so Medicare beneficiaries pay the lowest possible price, and it would have removed the legal preconditions that kept prescription drug imports from Canada from going forward. It also would have repealed Health Savings Accounts, phased down payments to private Medicare plans to match traditional Medicare rates, and required plans to disclose their drug coverage and costs to beneficiaries before they enroll.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors and disabled people on Medicare, who would pay less for prescriptions through government price negotiation and access to Canadian imports. Community pharmacies would gain from rules counting only storefront pharmacies toward access standards and from payments for counseling enrollees. People with multiple chronic conditions would get a funded care-coordination demonstration.

how_it_helps.text: Reverses the 2003 law's ban on government involvement in drug negotiations, giving the Secretary explicit authority to negotiate contracts with manufacturers so Part D enrollees 'pay the lowest possible price' [S2] [S3].

Strikes the requirement that the Secretary first prove importation's safety and savings to Congress, letting pharmacist and wholesaler imports from Canada proceed, and repeals the program's scheduled termination [S2] [S3].
Repeals the Health Savings Accounts created by the 2003 Medicare law, restoring prior law as if the provision had never passed [S3].

Phases private Medicare plan payments down to 100 percent of the traditional fee-for-service rate over five years, repeals the regional plan stabilization fund, and repeals the premium-support (competitive bidding) demonstration, all aimed at ending higher-than-traditional payments to private plans [S2] [S3].

Requires drug plans to disclose, on request, which drugs they cover, how their formulary and cost-sharing tiers work before a beneficiary enrolls, and to promptly notify enrollees of formulary changes [S2] [S3].

Funds a $1 billion, 10-site chronic care coordination demonstration (at least 4 rural sites, with one each in Arkansas and North Dakota) for beneficiaries with multiple chronic conditions, and expands a drug coverage demonstration nationwide with funding up to $2.1 billion [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would face government-negotiated prices and competition from Canadian imports on the new Part D market. Private insurers running Medicare Advantage and drug plans, whose payments would be phased down and who would lose the regional stabilization fund. Federal spending would rise for the $1 billion care-coordination and $2.1 billion drug-coverage demonstrations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and private Medicare insurers

drawbacks.text: Removing the requirement that the Secretary first certify the safety and consumer benefit of drug imports would let imports proceed without that safety review, the safeguard Congress had attached in 2003 [S2] [S3]. Critics of importation argue this raises the risk of unsafe or counterfeit medicines reaching consumers.

Cutting private plan payments to 100 percent of the fee-for-service rate and repealing the stabilization fund could lead some private plans to exit Medicare, reducing the plan choices the bill elsewhere tries to guarantee by requiring at least two drug plans per area [S2] [S3].
Repealing Health Savings Accounts takes away a tax-advantaged savings vehicle that some enrollees and employers had begun using, restoring the pre-2003 rules [S3].
The $1 billion demonstration is earmarked so that one site must be in Arkansas and one in North Dakota, the home states of the sponsor and cosponsor [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core provisions attack the two biggest criticisms of the 2003 drug benefit: a statutory bar on the government negotiating prices, and higher payments to private plans than traditional Medicare costs. Beneficiaries would likely pay less for drugs, though the importation change traded away a safety-certification step, and reduced private plan payments could shrink plan options. On balance the bill's benefits flow to Medicare beneficiaries and its costs to drug makers and private insurers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Kent Conrad introduced the bill in the Senate on April 22, 2004, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S1] [S5].
That referral was the last action of any kind; the Congress ended January 3, 2005 with no committee action, no floor vote, and no companion movement [S5].

The bill was written to amend provisions of the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003, which had barred the Secretary from interfering in negotiations between drug makers and plans and had conditioned Canadian drug importation on a certification to Congress [S2] [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept the ban on Medicare price negotiation and the barrier to Canadian imports, and private Medicare plans kept their higher payments and the regional stabilization fund. Medicare beneficiaries saw no change in drug prices or plan rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private Medicare insurers

for.name: Kent Conrad
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare Modernization Improvement Act of 2004 and delivered introductory remarks

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote during the remainder of the Congress

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: The industry publicly opposed government negotiation of Medicare drug prices and broad prescription drug importation, the bill's two central provisions

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat with two Democratic cosponsors, and it died without any action in a committee chaired by a Republican; no vote ever tested support across the chamber.

industries.note: The bill would end the 2003 law's bar on government price negotiation for the new Part D drug benefit and let drugs flow in from Canada, both of which would cut manufacturer prices and revenue on Medicare's largest new drug market. That cost is exactly the saving beneficiaries would capture.

industries.industry: Private Medicare Advantage and drug plan insurers
industries.note: Payment rates would be phased down to 100 percent of the traditional Medicare rate and the regional stabilization fund and premium-support program repealed, trimming plan revenue. At the same time, the bill would guarantee at least two drug plans per area and add a two-year federal fallback plan, and Medigap wraparound sales would open a new product line.

Only storefront pharmacies would count toward plans' convenient-access requirements, plans could not favor mail order over retail on amounts and refills, and pharmacies would receive payments (capped at $500 million) for counseling enrollees about their drug coverage. Seniors would get more local pharmacy access and face-to-face guidance.
The bill would let Medigap insurers sell approved wraparound drug coverage on top of the Part D benefit, a new market. Beneficiaries would gain an additional coverage option.

The bill repeals the Health Savings Accounts created by the 2003 Medicare law, eliminating the product for banks and administrators. The bill's premise was that HSAs mainly benefit higher-income and healthier enrollees rather than Medicare beneficiaries.
